title: What Dixieland means: syncopated marches
summary: Dickenson thinks the pieces called Dixieland were marches jazzed up with syncopation, different from ragtime.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Yeah. Well, they don't have to be Dixieland. So who said "Dixieland" anyhow? That's just some numbers...
They are just some numbers. Those pieces that they call Dixieland usually were marches. They were usually marches.
Well, when did that term come into general currency? Because it was pretty (?), I would say.
No, Dixieland, the way it's used now.

I don't know. I don't know. I guess they called it a Dixieland band. So what's a band? A band is a band that... I guess they used it for marching bands, you know, and... But they jazzed it up a little. [SINGS REFRAIN "HURRAY FOR THE RED, WHITE AND BLUE" STRAIGHT TIME, THEN SYNCOPATED] You know, syncopate the things a little. And that made it to be like, you know, struttin' sort of music, you know. That's mine. Don't take it from me that I'm right.
But it seems to me those numbers are like that, you know.
As opposed to maybe Ragtime, which were different numbers.
Well, Ragtime was another kind of music, I would think.
